tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. content.content:
99:Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed learning framework that enables clients to jointly optimize a common model through server coordination, while their local training data remain within their respective environments. Despite its privacy advantages, FL encounters significant challenges resulting from the participation of numerous clients having heterogeneous data during each training round. Consequently, this degrades accuracy, delays convergence, increases the communication overhead, and undermines fairness among participating clients. Hence, Client Selection (CS) has become essential for identifying the most beneficial clients for global model training. However, existing approaches often struggle to preserve model accuracy and fairness while limiting communication costs in the presence of non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data. In response to these challenges, we introduce FedFACS (Federated Fair Adaptive Client Selection), a novel framework designed to handle data heterogeneity while improving fairness and training efficiency. FedFACS formulates client selection using a multi-objective fitness function combining the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between local and global predictions with a dynamic fairness baseline. In addition, we incorporate an uncertainty-aware penalty that mitigates the impact of local noise. Moreover, a control mechanism is introduced to adaptively balance utility and fairness in response to global convergence feedback. A dynamic cohort sizing mechanism was developed that identifies the optimal number of high-fitness clients needed for each round. Furthermore, we propose a stability-weighted aggregation method that aligns model aggregation with the stability criteria. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets under several data heterogeneous settings show that FedFACS achieves average improvements of 1.39\% in accuracy, 1.41\% in F1-score, and 0.44\% in recall, as well as 3.47\% fewer selected clients while maintaining comparable communication rounds, in addition to improving fairness by an average of 1.38\% in Jain's Fairness Index (JFI), relative to the best performing existing method, thereby enhancing performance and reducing communication overhead while ensuring fairness.
135:Consequently, an effective client selection strategy is vital for identifying the most informative participants in each round contributes toward global model improvement, thereby limiting communication overhead (Asad et al. 2023), accelerating convergence, and enhancing performance. However, several client selection techniques rely on predefined participation ratios or fixed cohort sizes (Lai et al. 2021; Larsson et al. 2021). Such methods can result in the selection of participants that provide limited contributions to the global model. Other approaches are categorized as resource-based (Nishio and Yonetani 2019; Li et al. 2022), bandwidth-based (Ji et al. 2023), or correlation-based (Cho et al. 2022; Tang et al. 2021). However, most of these techniques fail to balance global and local factors, neglecting fair participation under non-IID data distributions. As a result, participants with larger datasets, better data quality, or stronger computational resources are repeatedly selected, while others remain idle for many rounds, which can bias the global model and affect generalization (Vucinich and Zhu 2023; Ayeelyan et al. 2025). Nonetheless, balancing performance and fairness in FL client selection under non-IID conditions is still an open challenge.
137:To overcome this limitation, we propose the Federated Fair Adaptive Client Selection (FedFACS) framework to harmonize the conflicts between fairness with predictive performance, communication efficiency, and convergence under diverse non-IID scenarios. FedFACS introduces a multi-dimensional selection fitness score that prioritizes clients offering the highest contribution to global model by leveraging three core factors: utility, fairness, and uncertainty penalty. Client utility is quantified by estimating its potential contribution to the global model through the KL divergence between local and global predictive distributions, which measures how far the local model has moved from the global model (Kullback and Leibler 1951). The uncertainty penalty is estimated using the variance of KL divergence measured across multiple mini-batches for each client. Fairness is quantified using normalized idle rounds, dynamically determined by the server, thereby reducing client domination (Shi et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024). Moreover, FedFACS balances utility and fairness using a bounded feedback control mechanism. The number of clients selected for aggregation (cohort size) is adaptively updated at every round in response to the current global model loss. Furthermore, the client contributions are quantified using stability score which is used to adaptively weight global model aggregation. The efficacy of FedFACS is demonstrated through rigorous evaluations across four benchmark datasets, outperforming competitive FL baselines across different data distribution settings. The key contributions of the proposed approach are summarized as follows:
139:\item Multi-Objective Fitness Function for Fair Adaptive Client Selection: We propose an adaptive client selection fitness function integrating KL-divergence-based client utility, an uncertainty penalty to improve robustness, and a dynamic fairness score for fair participation. Furthermore, the convergence progress of the global federated model guides the adjustment of fitness scores and determines the cohort size, thereby specifying the number of top-ranked clients selected for model aggregation in each training round. Specifically, the cohort size increases during convergence stagnation to encourage exploration and decreases during stable convergence under non-IID data settings to improve communication efficiency.
181:To address these limitations, an efficient client selection strategy is required to identify suitable clients for aggregation. Our proposed framework improves accuracy and scalability while minimizing communication overhead through fewer communication rounds and adaptive client cohort selection in each round. Furthermore, FedFACS integrates a suitable fairness mechanism to prevent the dominance of high-quality participants, prevent bias in the global model, and ensure fair client participation. It also incorporates an adaptive weighted aggregation method to maintain robustness and enhance performance under data heterogeneity distributions, addressing the limitations identified by previous studies.
202:At round $t$, the server selects a cohort $C_k^t \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ of size $m_t$ according to the fitness score of each client (Eq.~(14)). The cohort aims to maximize the total fitness, with ties broken by ascending client identifier, as in Eq.~(3), where $A$ is a candidate subset of $\mathcal{C}$, subject to the waiting-time guard of Section~\ref{sec:properties}. The terms of the fitness score are defined in Section 4.2.
209:To reduce upload traffic, the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ is adjusted dynamically from the convergence efficiency $\rho^{t-1}$ of the previous round (Eq.~(16)) and is bounded by $C_{k_{\min}} \le m_t \le C_{k_{\max}}$, where $C_{k_{\min}}$ and $C_{k_{\max}}$ are the lower and upper bounds, respectively.
235:Each training round $t$ proceeds as follows (Fig. 2). (Step 1) The coordinating server broadcasts the committed global model and the control state, namely the deviation signal $\nu^t$ (Eq. (10)) and the mean idle count $\overline{r^t}$ (Eq. (19)), to all $N$ candidate clients. (Step 2) Each candidate resets its local model to the global model, trains it for $E$ local epochs with learning rate $\eta$ on the loss of Eq. (2), and computes its composite fitness score on the same scoring examples, using the unchanged global model as reference. (Step 3) Each client transmits its composite fitness score; the server holds the number of consecutive idle rounds of every client. (Step 4) The server computes the cohort size $m_t$ from the convergence efficiency of the previous round and ranks the clients by fitness. (Step 5) The server selects the top-ranked $m_t$ clients $C_k^t$. (Step 6) The selected clients upload their trained parameters, raw stability score $s_i^t$ (Eq. (13)) and sample count $n_i$.
256:rounds across all clients, $\nu^{t}$: deviation control signal, $C^t_k \subset \mathcal{C}$: cohort selected by the server at round $t$
324:5.  & \hspace{2em}Compute the cohort size $m_t$ using (16) from $\rho^{t-1}$\\
341:Furthermore, algorithm 2 outlines the overall procedure of server-side client selection and model aggregation. Clients are ranked according to their fitness scores. In addition, the cohort size $m_t$ is dynamically defined from the global convergence efficiency of the previous round, and the cohort of $m_t$ clients is selected, overdue clients first and then those of highest fitness (Lines 3-6). The centralized server receives the trained models, stability scores and sample counts of the selected clients and combines them with the nonnegative stability weights of Eq. (18) to construct an aggregated global model for the subsequent training (Lines 7-8). Furthermore, the resulting candidate model is validated using the validation dataset (Line 9). The model, the feedback state and the idle counters are then committed together, and every participating client is supplied with the latest global model, accompanied by the fairness baseline and the deviation control signal (Lines 10-11).
376:The idle counter $r_i^t$ is the number of consecutive committed rounds before round $t$ in which client $i$ was not selected. It is held by the server and initialised as $r_i^1=0$ for all $i\in\mathcal{C}$. After each committed round it is updated by Eq.~(7), where $C_k^t$ denotes the cohort selected at round $t$; rounds whose staged state is discarded leave the counters unchanged.
454:On the server-side, it receives fitness scores from all clients for evaluation. The server ranks the clients according to their fitness scores and adaptively determines the cohort size $m_t=|C_k^t|$ according to the convergence efficiency observed in the previous communication round, namely the relative reduction $\rho^{t-1}$ of the validation loss as shown in Eq. (15). Two predefined integer bounds, $C_{k_{\min}}$ and $C_{k_{\max}}$ (fixed in advance for each configuration), regulate the allowable cohort size range (McMahan et al. 2017; Li et al. 2020), thereby enabling an adaptive number of clients to be selected for aggregation while maintaining communication efficiency and mitigating network congestion, as defined in Eq. (16). Here $L_{global}^{t}$ is the validation loss of the global model after round $t$ and $L_{global}^{0}$ that of the initial model; a negative $\rho^{t}$ records a loss increase and is retained, while a zero previous loss or a nonfinite value invalidates the round.
461:% REVISED (Replacement 7): integer cohort size within its bounds
467:When $\rho^{t-1}$ indicates sharp improvement, the cohort size is dynamically decreased reducing communication overhead. In contrast, during stagnation and degradation (including a loss increase), the cohort size increases to $C_{k_{\max}}$, requesting updates from more informative clients to improve global model accuracy and push it out of a local optimum; initialisation ($\rho^0=0$) also selects $C_{k_{\max}}$. The rule is a heuristic interpolation and is not shown to give a minimal or optimal cohort.
470:Once the selected clients submit their local updates, the stability scores are converted into aggregation weights. For the selected clients let $s_{i,+}^t=\max(s_i^t,0)$ be the positive part of the raw score and $H^t=\sum_{j\in C_k^t}s_{j,+}^t$ its cohort sum. Following this, the server carries out the aggregation, which is formulated as follows (Eq. (17) restates Eq. (4)):
499:This subsection states what the design guarantees. Throughout, $m_t=|C_k^t|$ is the cohort size of Eq.~(16) with $C_{k_{\min}}\le m_t\le C_{k_{\max}}$, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of $N$ clients and $r_i^t$ is the idle counter of Eq.~(7).
501:\textbf{Waiting-time guard.} To make participation fairness a guarantee rather than only a tendency of the fairness term, selection uses an age guard with threshold $R=\lceil N/C_{k_{\min}}\rceil$. Let $U^t=\{i\in\mathcal{C}: r_i^t\ge R\}$ be the overdue clients, ordered by decreasing $r_i^t$ and, for equal counters, by ascending identifier. If $|U^t|\ge m_t$, the cohort consists of the first $m_t$ clients of $U^t$; otherwise it consists of $U^t$ and of the $m_t-|U^t|$ clients of $\mathcal{C}\setminus U^t$ with the highest fitness (Eq.~(14)). When no client is overdue the rule is exactly Eq.~(3).
606:The relative contribution of each component in FedFACS is individually evaluated through a comprehensive ablation study. The components are the full FedFACS, FedFACS-A1 which removes both of adaptive aggregation and cohort sizing (Ablation 1), where client selection is performed with a constant sampling size of ($C_k^t=10$) and static weighted aggregation is used (McMahan et al. 2017), and FedFACS-A2 that utilizing dynamic cohort sizing with ($C_{k_{\min}} = 8$) and ($C_{k_{\max}} = 10$) removes adaptive aggregation only (Ablation 2). The experimental setup follows configuration A, and The target accuracy is determined as the maximum accuracy obtained by FedAvg under the corresponding experiments with data partitioning conditions presented in scenarios 1 and 2.
608:Tables 1 and 2 demonstrate the improvements achieved by FedFACS-A1 that incorporates the proposed adaptive client selection mechanism, including higher predictive accuracy while reducing the communication rounds required to attain the target accuracy. Moreover, introducing dynamic cohort sizing in FedFACS-A2 leads to a slight change in accuracy due to the adaptive reduction in participating clients, and reduces communication overhead by selecting approximately 15\% fewer clients per training round. Furthermore, incorporating the adaptive stability-weighted aggregation in the full FedFACS model limits the effect of gradient noise from unstable clients by assigning larger aggregation weights to stable and informative client updates. Consequently, the aggregated global model becomes more robust, mitigating the impact of noisy clients and accelerating convergence with fewer training rounds.
1129:This is achieved through the integration of fitness-based client selection, adaptive cohort sizing, and stability-weighted aggregation, which enhance the effectiveness of federated learning under heterogeneous data distributions, facilitate faster convergence, and enable more efficient utilization of participating clients. Consequently, FedFACS is well suited to practical federated learning environments with limited communication resources. 
1202:As depicted in Fig.~10, FedFACS improves fairness compared with the best-performing baseline, FairFedCS, achieving average \textit{JFI} improvements of approximately 1.29\% on CIFAR-10 and 1.47\% on FMNIST. FedFACS achieves slightly higher \textit{JFI} values than FairFedCS in most scenarios, with gains ranging from (+0.006) to (+0.026) as shown in Fig. 11. 135:Consequently, an effective client selection strategy is vital for identifying the most informative participants in each round contributes toward global model improvement, thereby limiting communication overhead (Asad et al. 2023), accelerating convergence, and enhancing performance. However, several client selection techniques rely on predefined participation ratios or fixed cohort sizes (Lai et al. 2021; Larsson et al. 2021). Such methods can result in the selection of participants that provide limited contributions to the global model. Other approaches are categorized as resource-based (Nishio and Yonetani 2019; Li et al. 2022), bandwidth-based (Ji et al. 2023), or correlation-based (Cho et al. 2022; Tang et al. 2021). However, most of these techniques fail to balance global and local factors, neglecting fair participation under non-IID data distributions. As a result, participants with larger datasets, better data quality, or stronger computational resources are repeatedly selected, while others remain idle for many rounds, which can bias the global model and affect generalization (Vucinich and Zhu 2023; Ayeelyan et al. 2025). Nonetheless, balancing performance and fairness in FL client selection under non-IID conditions is still an open challenge.
137:To overcome this limitation, we propose the Federated Fair Adaptive Client Selection (FedFACS) framework to harmonize the conflicts between fairness with predictive performance, communication efficiency, and convergence under diverse non-IID scenarios. Client utility is quantified by estimating its potential contribution to the global model through the KL divergence between local and global predictive distributions, which measures how far the local model has moved from the global model (Kullback and Leibler 1951). The uncertainty penalty is estimated using the variance of KL divergence measured across multiple mini-batches for each client. Fairness is quantified using normalized idle rounds, dynamically determined by the server, thereby reducing client domination (Shi et al. 2024; Xu et al. 2024). 131	    a, b = parse_block(orig, onums), parse_block(rev, rnums)
132	    sm = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, [key(u) for u in a], [key(u) for u in b], autojunk=False)

135	        if op in ("delete", "replace"):
136	            da.update(range(i1, i2))
137	        if op in ("insert", "replace"):
138	            db.update(range(j1, j2))

151	    b = min(x for x in (b1 + 1 if b1 >= 0 else len(text), b2 if b2 >= 0 else len(text)))

"""Builds FedFACS_Replacements_5_6.docx (Before/After with locations, declarations, evidence tables, notation).
Sources: paper_overleaf/sn-article.tex (original), paper_overleaf_revised/sn-article.tex (revised),
paper_overleaf_revised/section_5_4_selection_score.tex (new subsection). Native Word equations via pandoc."""
import difflib
import os
import re
import subprocess

import docx
import pypandoc
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.shared import Inches, Pt, RGBColor

P = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper"
OUT = os.path.join(P, "FedFACS_Replacements_5_6.docx")
WORK = os.path.join(P, "tools", "_work")
os.makedirs(WORK, exist_ok=True)
ORIG = open(os.path.join(P, "paper_overleaf", "sn-article.tex"), encoding="utf8", newline="").read().replace("\r\n", "\n")
REV = open(os.path.join(P, "paper_overleaf_revised", "sn-article.tex"), encoding="utf8", newline="").read().replace("\r\n", "\n")
S54 = open(os.path.join(P, "paper_overleaf_revised", "section_5_4_selection_score.tex"), encoding="utf8", newline="").read().replace("\r\n", "\n")
BS = chr(92)
BSR = re.escape(BS)

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- LaTeX -> markdown helpers
MATH = re.compile(r"(\$[^$]+\$)")


def conv_text(s):
    out = []
    for k, part in enumerate(MATH.split(s)):
        if k % 2 == 1:
            out.append(part.replace(BS + BS + "[1.5ex]", BS + BS))
            continue
        t = part
        t = t.replace(BS + "ref{sec:properties}", "4.3").replace(BS + "ref{sec:score_analysis}", "5.4")
        t = t.replace(BS + "ref{tab:mixing}", "Y").replace(BS + "ref{tab:kl_validity}", "X").replace(BS + "ref{tab:kl_drift}", "X2")
        t = re.sub(BSR + r"ref\{([^}]*)\}", r"\1", t)
        t = t.replace("_", BS + "_")
        t = re.sub(BSR + r"textbf\{([^}]*)\}", r"**\1**", t)
        t = re.sub(BSR + r"textit\{([^}]*)\}", r"*\1*", t)
        t = t.replace(BS + "%", "%").replace("~", " ").replace("--", "\u2013").replace("``", "\u201c").replace("''", "\u201d")
        out.append(t)
    return "".join(out)


TOK = re.compile(r"\$[^$]+\$[^\s$]*|\S+")


def eq_clean(body):
    body = re.sub(BSR + r"label\{[^}]*\}", "", body)
    body = re.sub(BSR + r"tag\{[^}]*\}", "", body)
    body = body.replace(BS + BS + "[1.5ex]", BS + BS)
    return body.strip()


def eq_norm(body):
    return re.sub(r"\s+", "", eq_clean(body))


def parse_block(text, nums):
    nums = list(nums)
    units = []
    pos = 0

    def text_units(t):
        t = "\n".join(l for l in t.split("\n") if not l.lstrip().startswith("%"))
        paras = [p for p in re.split(r"\n\s*\n", t) if p.strip()]
        for i, p in enumerate(paras):
            if i:
                units.append(("P",))
            for tok in TOK.findall(p):
                units.append(("T", tok))

    for m in re.finditer(BSR + r"begin\{equation\}(.*?)" + BSR + r"end\{equation\}", text, re.S):
        text_units(text[pos:m.start()])
        units.append(("E", eq_norm(m.group(1)), eq_clean(m.group(1)), nums.pop(0)))
        pos = m.end()
    text_units(text[pos:])
    assert not nums, nums
    return units


def key(u):
    return u[1] if u[0] == "E" else ("\u00b6" if u[0] == "P" else u[1])


def render(units, marks, style_inline, style_block):
    """markdown for a unit list; marks = set of indexes to highlight."""
    lines, para = [], []
    state = {"run": []}

    def flush_run():
        if state["run"]:
            para.append('[%s]{custom-style="%s"}' % (" ".join(state["run"]), style_inline))
            state["run"] = []

    def flush_para():
        flush_run()
        if para:
            lines.append(" ".join(para))
            lines.append("")
            para.clear()

    for i, u in enumerate(units):
        if u[0] == "P":
            flush_para()
        elif u[0] == "E":
            flush_para()
            md = "$$ %s \\qquad (%s) $$" % (u[2], u[3])
            if i in marks:
                lines.append('::: {custom-style="%s"}' % style_block)
                lines.append(md)
                lines.append(":::")
            else:
                lines.append(md)
            lines.append("")
        else:
            c = conv_text(u[1])
            if i in marks:
                state["run"].append(c)
            else:
                flush_run()
                para.append(c)
    flush_para()
    return "\n".join(lines)


def before_after(orig, rev, onums, rnums):
    a, b = parse_block(orig, onums), parse_block(rev, rnums)
    sm = difflib.SequenceMatcher(None, [key(u) for u in a], [key(u) for u in b], autojunk=False)
    da, db = set(), set()
    for op, i1, i2, j1, j2 in sm.get_opcodes():
        if op in ("delete", "replace"):
            da.update(range(i1, i2))
        if op in ("insert", "replace"):
            db.update(range(j1, j2))
    return render(a, da, "Del", "DelBlock"), render(b, db, "Add", "AddBlock")


def line_of(text, sub):
    return text.count("\n", 0, text.index(sub)) + 1


def sentence(text, k):
    i = text.index(k)
    a = max(text.rfind(". ", 0, i) + 2 if text.rfind(". ", 0, i) >= 0 else 0, text.rfind("\n", 0, i) + 1)
    b1 = text.find(". ", i)
    b2 = text.find("\n", i)
    b = min(x for x in (b1 + 1 if b1 >= 0 else len(text), b2 if b2 >= 0 else len(text)))
    return text[a:b]


def span(text, start, end, from_marker=None):
    i = text.index(from_marker or start)
    j = text.index(end, i) + len(end)
    return text[i:j]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- the seven edits
EQ_END = lambda lab: BS + "label{" + lab + "}\n" + BS + "end{equation}"
EDITS = [
    dict(rep=5, title="Abstract: wording of the KL utility", loc="Abstract (original line %d)",
         orig=sentence(ORIG, "multi-objective fitness function combining"), rev=sentence(REV, "multi-objective fitness function combining"),
         onums=[], rnums=[], at=("multi-objective fitness function combining", ORIG)),
    dict(rep=5, title="Introduction: definition of the client utility", loc="Section 1, contributions paragraph (original line %d)",
         orig=sentence(ORIG, "Client utility is quantified by"), rev=sentence(REV, "Client utility is quantified by"),
         onums=[], rnums=[], at=("Client utility is quantified by", ORIG)),
    dict(rep=5, title="Section 4.2: KL score, Eqs. (5a), (5b), (5), and its effect on the priority", loc="Section 4.2, first paragraph and Eq. (5) (original line %d)",
         orig=span(ORIG, EQ_END("eq:kl"), EQ_END("eq:kl"), "Each participating client is denoted by"),
         rev=span(REV, "keeps every client participating.", "keeps every client participating.", "% REVISED (Replacement 5): KL"),
         onums=["5"], rnums=["5a", "5b", "5"], at=("Each participating client is denoted by", ORIG)),
    dict(rep=5, title="Section 4.2: uncertainty penalty, stability score and fitness, Eqs. (12a), (12), (13), (14)", loc="Section 4.2 (original line %d)",
         orig=span(ORIG, EQ_END("eq:fitness"), EQ_END("eq:fitness"), "Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score"),
         rev=span(REV, EQ_END("eq:fitness"), EQ_END("eq:fitness"), "% REVISED (Replacement 5/6): batch variance"),
         onums=["12", "13", "14"], rnums=["12a", "12", "13", "14"], at=("Client-side uncertainty is introduced into the fitness score", ORIG)),
    dict(rep=6, title="Introduction: wording of the control mechanism", loc="Section 1, contributions paragraph (original line %d)",
         orig=sentence(ORIG, "FedFACS balances utility and fairness using a"), rev=sentence(REV, "FedFACS balances utility and fairness using a"),
         onums=[], rnums=[], at=("FedFACS balances utility and fairness using a", ORIG)),
    dict(rep=6, title="Section 4.2: feedback rule and priority, Eqs. (8) and (9)", loc="Section 4.2 (original line %d)",
         orig=span(ORIG, EQ_END("eq:priority"), EQ_END("eq:priority"), "The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov"),
         rev=span(REV, EQ_END("eq:priority"), EQ_END("eq:priority"), "% REVISED (Replacement 6)"),
         onums=["8", "9"], rnums=["8", "9"], at=("The proposed control mechanism is inspired by the Lyapunov", ORIG)),
]

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- narrative blocks
HEAD = r"""
::: {custom-style="BA-Title"}
FedFACS: Replacements 5 and 6 (final text, declarations and evidence)
:::

Scope. Replacement 5 covers the utility score, the uncertainty penalty and the fitness (Eqs. (5), (12)–(14)); Replacement 6 covers the feedback rule and the priority (Eqs. (8)–(9)). Locations refer to the original sn-article.tex. Evidence comes from our reproduced runs (ResNet-18 with frozen early layers, 100 clients, 100 rounds, cohorts of 5 to 10 clients; 3 seeds for ablations, 5 for the main comparison, 2 for the parameter-drift study; 95% bootstrap intervals); the manuscript must state that its numbers come from this implementation. Colours: [red]{custom-style="Del"} = removed, [green]{custom-style="Add"} = added.
:::

::: {custom-style="BA-Note"}
Consequence for Replacements 8–9. Eq. (18) is generalised with a coefficient κ: κ = 0 gives sample-count weights and κ = 1 the stability weights. All reported results use κ = 0, because stability weights increased the oscillation of the global model at the end of training (Section 5.4, Aggregation weights). The wording of Replacements 8–9, the abstract and the conclusion must follow this choice.
:::

# 1. What each comment receives: fix, location, evidence, declaration
"""

COMMENTS = [
    ("R1-04 and R2-06: the utility score and its sum over x ∈ X",
     "Eq. (5) is replaced by a three-level definition: per-example divergence over the label set (5a), batch mean (5b) and sample-weighted client score (5). The text states what a large and a small value mean and how the score enters the priority.",
     "Section 4.2, Eqs. (5a), (5b), (5); Abstract and Introduction wording.",
     "New subsection 5.4: rank correlation of the score with the marginal validation-loss gain (Table X), comparison with the global cross-entropy and with the parameter drift (Tables X and X2), behaviour under label noise.",

REP6_ONLY = True
HEAD6 = r"""

PREP6 = r"""

Dear Authors, I recommend Reject for the present submission to the Journal of King Saud University Computer and Information Sciences. The manuscript addresses a relevant problem: balancing predictive performance, client participation fairness, and communication requirements in federated learning under heterogeneous data distributions. Combining client utility, participation history, uncertainty penalties, adaptive cohort sizing, and aggregation weights is potentially useful, and the evaluation across four datasets provides a reasonable starting point. However, the current submission contains fundamental inconsistencies in the fairness mechanism, control update, aggregation rule, and interpretation of communication efficiency. The experimental reporting also leaves substantial uncertainty about implementation correctness, reproducibility, and the significance of the reported improvements. These concerns affect the central contribution rather than only its presentation.
My first concern is that the stated fairness mechanism does not implement the behavior described in the manuscript. Equation (7) resets the idle-round counter to zero when a client is selected but leaves it unchanged when the client is not selected. Consequently, with zero initialization, every counter remains zero throughout training, and Equation (6) gives the same fairness value of one for every client. This contradicts the repeated explanation that fairness priority increases as a client remains unselected. Please establish whether the implementation increments the counter for an unselected client and whether Equation (7) is a transcription error. The counter initialization, update timing, and calculation of the population average must be specified consistently. This distinction is essential because the reported fairness improvements cannot presently be attributed to the mechanism as written.
The adaptive control law in Equation (8) is also not well-defined over the stated operating conditions. Its denominator contains the sum of a fairness regularization term and the signed quantity \(\nu^t(\Delta KL_i^t-F_i^t)\), which can be zero or arbitrarily close to zero. Downlink and local-compute costs must be reported; otherwise the “communication-efficient” claim is misleading and the comparison is unfair.

Calling it “Lyapunov-inspired” is unjustified without a Lyapunov function or a stability proof; as written it is a smoothed heuristic.

R1-03 The adaptive control law in Equation (8) is also not well-defined over the stated operating conditions. Its denominator contains the sum of a fairness regularization term and the signed quantity \(\nu^t(\Delta KL_i^t-F_i^t)\), which can be zero or arbitrarily close to zero. Projection onto \([0,1]\) after evaluating the fraction does not resolve an undefined division. Furthermore, the explanation that a positive deviation signal increases the utility weight does not follow generally from this equation. When the utility term is smaller than the fairness term, a positive deviation can instead decrease the utility weight. Please define the unindexed \(F\), establish the admissible parameter and signal ranges, and demonstrate the intended directional behavior. Describing the mechanism as Lyapunov-inspired does not establish stability, and bounding one mixing coefficient does not establish stable global training. Either provide an appropriate analysis or present the controller as a heuristic with explicitly tested limitations.

R1-06 The uncertainty penalty needs a similarly careful interpretation. Equation (12) measures variation in KL divergence across mini-batches. Such variation does not distinguish noisy data from legitimate heterogeneity, rare classes, or differences in mini-batch composition. Conversely, a consistently misleading client can have low between-batch variance. Please test whether the penalty discriminates corrupted updates from useful but heterogeneous updates, rather than assuming that low variance establishes reliability. The manuscript should disclose the number of scoring batches, their sampling procedure, and the handling of clients with fewer than two batches, for which the displayed sample-variance formula is undefined. Sensitivity to batch size and the penalty coefficient is necessary because both selection and aggregation depend on this quantity.

R1-11 The claims of preventing client starvation and preserving model fairness exceed the supplied evidence. Even with a corrected idle-round counter, the utility–fairness coefficient can reach one and remove the fairness term from the priority score. Moreover, selecting a client does not ensure that it meaningfully influences the model when its aggregation weight can be negligible or negative. Please report selection-frequency distributions, the proportion of clients never selected, maximum waiting times, and cumulative aggregation influence. Per-client or worst-performing-client predictive results would also help determine whether participation improvements translate into more equitable model performance. Without these analyses or a formal guarantee, the manuscript should describe empirical changes in the specified participation metric rather than claiming that starvation and model bias are prevented.

R1-18 The COVID-19 experiment requires additional dataset and evaluation documentation. The dataset is described as having three classes, whereas the model description states that the final layer is adjusted for ten classes. Please reconcile these statements and report the exact dataset version, selected classes, sample counts, and training, validation, and test partitions. Describe any patient-level grouping, duplicate checks, and source separation used to prevent overlap between evaluation partitions. The manuscript should also identify whether recall and F1-score are macro-averaged, micro-averaged, support-weighted, or calculated for a particular class. Aggregate results alone do not support the broader medical-imaging reliability statements, particularly because Table 4 reports lower recall for FedFACS than AHIBCS on this dataset.

R2-07 7. Aggregation weights (Eqs. 4, 13, 17–18). s = ΔKL − μσ² can be negative, yielding negative aggregation weights. Dataset size n_i is dropped, which is inconsistent with the objective in Eq. 1. Eq. 4 is unnormalized while Eq. 17 is normalized.

R2-08 8. Inconsistent time indexing and bounds. ν^{t+1} = Ω^{t+1} − ρ^{t+1} requires future losses. Eqs. 10 and 15–16 mix ρ^t and ρ^{t−1}. If ρ < 0, then (1 − ρ) > 1 and C_k^t exceeds C_kmax. Rounding of the cohort size and the treatment of rounds 1–2 are unspecified. Notation (N/K/C) is inconsistent.

R2-09 9. Negligible dynamic range of the cohort. The cohort varies only within 8–10 clients (C_kmin = 8, C_kmax = 10), so the claimed communication savings are inherently small. The reported “≈15% fewer clients per round” (Ablation 2) is impossible with these bounds (maximum 20%) and inconsistent with Fig. 4 and Table 3, where average cohort sizes are ≈9.6–9.97.

R2-10 10. Numerical inconsistencies in the experiments.

def run_metrics(r, target=None):
    lg = r["log"]
    va, ta = np.array(lg["val_acc"]), np.array(lg["test_acc"])
    sc = np.array(r["sel_count"], float)
    noise = np.array(r.get("noise", np.zeros(len(sc))))
    q = 10.0 * (1.0 - noise)
    pc = np.array(r["per_client_acc"])
    cm = np.array(r["confusion"], float)
    tp = np.diag(cm)
    rec = tp / np.maximum(cm.sum(1), 1)
    prec = tp / np.maximum(cm.sum(0), 1)
    f1 = 2 * prec * rec / np.maximum(prec + rec, 1e-12)
    m = dict(acc_best=ta[int(va.argmax())] * 100, acc_last10=ta[-10:].mean() * 100, acc_final=ta[-1] * 100,
             val_best=va.max() * 100, macro_recall=rec.mean() * 100, macro_prec=prec.mean() * 100, macro_f1=f1.mean() * 100,
             acc_from_cm=tp.sum() / cm.sum() * 100,
             jfi=jain(sc), jfi_q=jain(sc / q), never=(sc == 0).mean() * 100, max_wait=max(r["max_wait"]),
             pc_mean=pc.mean() * 100, pc_std=pc.std() * 100, pc_p10=np.percentile(pc, 10) * 100,
             cohort=np.mean(lg["cohort"]), up_gb=lg["up"][-1] / 1e9, down_gb=lg["down"][-1] / 1e9,
             steps_m=lg["steps"][-1] / 1e6, wall=np.mean(lg["wall"]), peak_mb=r.get("peak_mem_mb", np.nan),
             clip=r.get("clip_hits", 0), failed=r.get("failed_updates", 0), invalid=r.get("invalid_rounds", 0),
             jitter=np.abs(np.diff(ta[-30:])).mean() * 100)
    if target is not None:
        hit = np.where(va >= target)[0]
        rr = int(hit[0]) + 1 if len(hit) else None
        m["r2t"] = rr
        for k in ("up", "down"):
            m[k + "_gb_r2t"] = lg[k][rr - 1] / 1e9 if rr else None
        m["steps_m_r2t"] = lg["steps"][rr - 1] / 1e6 if rr else None
    return m


def ms(x, fmt="{:.2f}"):
    x = np.array([v for v in x if v is not None and not (isinstance(v, float) and np.isnan(v))], float)

"""Evidence for Replacements 7 (cohort) and 8 (aggregation), computed from the reproduced runs only."""
import collections
import glob
import json
import os

import numpy as np

R = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\fedfacs_repro\results"
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)


def boot(x, n=4000):
    x = np.array(x, float)
    b = [rng.choice(x, len(x)).mean() for _ in range(n)]
    return x.mean(), np.percentile(b, 2.5), np.percentile(b, 97.5)


def load(pat):
    return [json.load(open(f)) for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(R, pat)))]


A2 = load("*_abl_A2_s*.json")
FF = load("*_fedfacs_s*.json")
print("A2 runs", len(A2), "FedFACS runs", len(FF))
for name, rs in (("A2", A2), ("FedFACS", FF)):
    m = [np.mean(r["log"]["cohort"]) for r in rs]
    mean, lo, hi = boot(m)
    print(name, "mean cohort %.2f [%.2f, %.2f]  saving vs 10: %.1f%% [%.1f, %.1f]" % (mean, lo, hi, 100 * (1 - mean / 10), 100 * (1 - hi / 10), 100 * (1 - lo / 10)))
    allc = np.concatenate([r["log"]["cohort"] for r in rs]).astype(int)
    print("  histogram of m_t (0..10):", np.bincount(allc, minlength=11).tolist(), " min", allc.min(), " cmin cfg", set(r["cfg"]["cmin"] for r in rs))
    print("  rounds with m_t=cmax: %.0f%%" % (100 * (allc == 10).mean()))
    print("  invalid rounds:", sum(r["invalid_rounds"] for r in rs), " failed updates:", sum(r["failed_updates"] for r in rs))
# per scenario A2
S = collections.defaultdict(list)
for r in A2:
    c = r["cfg"]
    S[(c["dataset"], c["scenario"])].append(np.mean(r["log"]["cohort"]))
print("per cell A2 mean cohort:", {k: round(float(np.mean(v)), 2) for k, v in sorted(S.items())})
# rounds with cohort below 8 in FedFACS (where and why)
low = [(r["cfg"]["dataset"], r["cfg"]["scenario"], r["cfg"]["seed"], int(min(r["log"]["cohort"])), r["failed_updates"]) for r in FF if min(r["log"]["cohort"]) < r["cfg"]["cmin"]]
print("FedFACS runs with a round below cmin:", len(low), low[:5])
# weights
wm = [min(r["log"]["weights_min"]) for r in FF]
print("min aggregation weight, FedFACS (stability): %.3g ; A2: %.3g" % (min(wm), min(min(r["log"]["weights_min"]) for r in A2)))
# cumulative aggregation influence under sample-count weights (A2): sum over rounds of n_i / sum n_sel
def influence(r):
    n = np.array(r["n"], float)
    infl = np.zeros(len(n))
    for sel in r["log"]["selected"]:
        sel = list(sel)
        if not sel:
            continue
        infl[sel] += n[sel] / n[sel].sum()
    return infl


def gini(x):
    x = np.sort(np.asarray(x, float))
    n = len(x)
    return float((2 * np.arange(1, n + 1) - n - 1).dot(x) / (n * x.sum()))


rows = []
for r in A2:
    i = influence(r)
    rows.append((np.mean(i == 0) * 100, i.min() / i.mean(), i.max() / i.mean(), gini(i)))
rows = np.array(rows)
print("A2 cumulative aggregation influence: share of clients with zero influence %.2f%%, min/mean %.2f, max/mean %.2f, Gini %.3f" % tuple(rows.mean(0)))

    """Eq. (rho): validation-loss reduction of a completed round; invalid inputs raise."""

        raise ValueError("invalid loss pair for rho: %r, %r" % (L_prev, L_curr))

def omega_nu_next(t, omega_t, rho_hist, beta_ref=0.9):
    """After committed round t return (Omega^{t+1}, nu^{t+1}).

    rho_hist[k] = rho^k with rho_hist[0] = 0 (rho^0). Eq. (omega): Omega^2 = 0 and
    Omega^{t+1} = beta_ref*Omega^t + (1-beta_ref)*rho^{t-1} for t >= 2. Eq. (nu):
    nu^{t+1} = Omega^{t+1} - rho^t.
    """
    if t == 1:
        om = 0.0
    else:
        om = beta_ref * omega_t + (1.0 - beta_ref) * rho_hist[t - 1]
    return om, om - rho_hist[t]

"""Run one experiment: python run.py --dataset cifar10 --scenario s1_0.5 --method fedfacs --seed 0"""
import argparse
import json
import os
import sys

RESULTS = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "results")


def default_cfg(**kw):
    cfg = dict(dataset="cifar10", scenario="s1_0.5", method="fedfacs", seed=0, N=100, rounds=100, epochs=2,
               bs=32, lr=None, m=10, cmin=5, cmax=10, B=4, S=256, beta=0.9, lam=1.0, beta_ref=0.9,
               prox=0.1, d=20, clip=50.0, mu=None, diag_rounds=[])
    cfg.update(kw)
    if cfg["lr"] is None:
        cfg["lr"] = 0.05 if cfg["dataset"] == "cifar10" else 0.01
    return cfg


def result_path(cfg, tag=""):
    name = f"{cfg['dataset']}_{cfg['scenario']}_{cfg['method']}_s{cfg['seed']}{tag}.json"
    return os.path.join(RESULTS, name)


def run_one(cfg, tag="", verbose=True, force=False):
    import torch
    from fl import Sim
    path = result_path(cfg, tag)
    if os.path.exists(path) and not force:
        print("skip (exists):", path, flush=True)
        return path
    os.makedirs(RESULTS, exist_ok=True)
    sim = Sim(cfg)
    out = sim.run(cfg["method"], verbose=verbose)
    out["cfg"] = cfg
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(out, f)
    del sim
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return path

               bs=32, lr=None, m=10, cmin=5, cmax=10, B=4, S=256, beta=0.9, lam=1.0, beta_ref=0.9,

    return cfg


def result_path(cfg, tag=""):
    name = f"{cfg['dataset']}_{cfg['scenario']}_{cfg['method']}_s{cfg['seed']}{tag}.json"
    return os.path.join(RESULTS, name)


def run_one(cfg, tag="", verbose=True, force=False):
    import torch
    from fl import Sim
    path = result_path(cfg, tag)
    if os.path.exists(path) and not force:
        print("skip (exists):", path, flush=True)
        return path
    os.makedirs(RESULTS, exist_ok=True)
    sim = Sim(cfg)
    out = sim.run(cfg["method"], verbose=verbose)
    out["cfg"] = cfg
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        json.dump(out, f)
    del sim
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
    return path

"""Resumable sweep driver. python sweep.py <plan.json>

plan = {"rounds", "epochs", "datasets", "scenarios", "methods", "seeds", "tag", "extra": {cfg overrides},
        "grid": [{"tag": "_B2", "extra": {"B": 2}}, ...]}      # grid optional: one run set per grid point
Runs are sequential inside one worker; finished runs are skipped, so a crashed worker can simply be restarted.
A failed job is logged and skipped (it never stops the worker).
"""
import json
import sys
import time
import traceback

from run import default_cfg, run_one

if __name__ == "__main__":
    plan = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
    grids = plan.get("grid") or [{"tag": plan.get("tag", ""), "extra": {}}]
    jobs = [(g, d, s, m, seed) for seed in plan["seeds"] for g in grids for d in plan["datasets"]
            for s in plan["scenarios"] for m in plan["methods"]]
    print(f"{len(jobs)} jobs", flush=True)
    t0, failed = time.time(), []
    for k, (g, d, s, m, seed) in enumerate(jobs, 1):
        extra = {**plan.get("extra", {}), **g.get("extra", {})}
        cfg = default_cfg(dataset=d, scenario=s, method=m, seed=seed, rounds=plan["rounds"],
                          epochs=plan["epochs"], **extra)
        t1 = time.time()
        try:
            run_one(cfg, g.get("tag", plan.get("tag", "")), verbose=False)
            print(f"[{k}/{len(jobs)}] {d} {s} {m} seed={seed}{g.get('tag', '')} done in {time.time() - t1:.0f}s "
                  f"(elapsed {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min)", flush=True)
        except Exception:
            failed.append((d, s, m, seed, g.get("tag", "")))
            print(f"[{k}/{len(jobs)}] FAILED {d} {s} {m} seed={seed}{g.get('tag', '')}", flush=True)
            traceback.print_exc()
    print("FAILED JOBS:", failed, flush=True)
    print("ALL DONE", flush=True)

759 An overview of the experimental results obtained by FedFACS on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and FMNIST is presented in Table 3 and Fig. 3, illustrating its capability to achieve higher accuracy with fewer communication rounds, while Fig. 4 indicates the cumulative number of participating clients. All the experiments follow configuration A under non-IID settings defined by data partitioning 

881 For the CIFAR-10 dataset, FedFACS achieves accuracies of 47.07\%, 51.12\%, and 47.33\% after 200 training rounds under different data partitioning conditions as illustrated in Fig. 5. FedFACS achieves the best classification accuracy among the baseline methods by 0.48\%, 0.89\%, and 0.67\% increases over the best-performing method. Moreover, Table 3 reports the communication overhead in terms of communication round count required to achieve a predefined accuracy, where the target accuracies were configured to 44\%, 48\%, and 44\% across the three data distribution scenarios.

884 In comparison with the baseline approaches, FedFACS accelerates convergence, requiring approximately 40, 57, and 110 rounds to attain the target accuracy under the three non-IID conditions, respectively, representing reductions of approximately 9\%, 8\%, and 2.6\% in communication rounds compared with Zhai et al. (2024). The observed reduction in communication rounds depends on the level of data skewness across the evaluated scenarios, reflecting the effectiveness of the adaptive control mechanism. The 9\% and 8\% improvements are achieved in more stable scenarios, where FedFACS rapidly identifies informative clients and eliminates redundant communication rounds, while in the more challenging scenario with a 2.6\% improvement, the convergence slows due to severe data heterogeneity where clients hold underrepresented classes which leads to a slower aggregation process to ensure stable convergence over additional rounds. In addition, FedFACS reduces the communication overhead not only by achieving the target accuracy in fewer communication rounds, but also by requiring a lower cumulative count of clients involved in aggregation, with approximately $4\%-12.5\%$ fewer clients than the best-performing baseline as demonstrated in Fig. 4(a). As a result, the overall communication overhead associated with data transmission is reduced. 

886 Furthermore, FedFACS records the highest average accuracies of 98.52\%, 98.91\%, and 98.11\%, with corresponding improvements of 0.27\%, 0.31\%, and 0.22\% over the best-performing method under the three data distribution conditions, as shown in Fig. 6. Moreover, FedFACS attains the predefined target accuracies of 97\%, 98\%, and 97\% within approximately 58, 69, and 115 communication rounds as presented in Table 3, demonstrating a reduction in communication overhead compared with Zhai et al. (2024) for the first two distribution conditions by 14.7\% and 5.4\%, while selecting approximately $7\%-17\%$ fewer clients as illustrated in Fig. 4(b). However, no much improvement is observed under the data partitioning of scenario 2. In addition, DivFL is 2x faster than the proposed framework with fewer selected clients under the first data distribution scenario. Nevertheless, FedFACS sacrifices communication efficiency to ensure fairness and achieves higher final accuracy compared with DivFL by 1.19\%, 0.74\%, and 1.98\% across the three distribution conditions.

890 Finally, FedFACS achieves the highest average accuracies of 86.63\%, 88.95\%, and 83.08\% under varying data distribution conditions. Relative to the best baseline approach, these outcomes show increases of 0.35\% and 0.85\% under the first two distribution conditions, while a slight decrease of 0.2\% in the third condition, as illustrated in Fig. 7. Furthermore, the proposed framework reaches the predefined target accuracies of 84\%, 87\%, and 80\% within 81, 99, and 105 corresponding training rounds. This demonstrates an enhanced communication efficiency compared with the best-performing baseline, Zhai et al. (2024) by selecting $2.3\%-5.8\%$ fewer clients, as shown in Fig. 4(c) and requiring approximately 4.7\%, 2\%, and 2.2\% fewer communication rounds as presented in Table 3.

\subsection{Properties of FedFACS}\label{sec:properties}
This subsection states what the design guarantees. Throughout, $m_t=|C_k^t|$ is the cohort size of Eq.~(16) with $C_{k_{\min}}\le m_t\le C_{k_{\max}}$, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of $N$ clients and $r_i^t$ is the idle counter of Eq.~(7).

\textbf{Waiting-time guard.} To make participation fairness a guarantee rather than only a tendency of the fairness term, selection uses an age guard with threshold $R=\lceil N/C_{k_{\min}}\rceil$. Let $U^t=\{i\in\mathcal{C}: r_i^t\ge R\}$ be the overdue clients, ordered by decreasing $r_i^t$ and, for equal counters, by ascending identifier. If $|U^t|\ge m_t$, the cohort consists of the first $m_t$ clients of $U^t$; otherwise it consists of $U^t$ and of the $m_t-|U^t|$ clients of $\mathcal{C}\setminus U^t$ with the highest fitness (Eq.~(14)). When no client is overdue the rule is exactly Eq.~(3).

\textbf{Proposition 1 (well-posedness).} In every round: (i) the denominator of Eq.~(8) is at least $\lambda>0$ and $a_i^t\in[0,1]$; (ii) $1\le F_i^t<N+1$; (iii) $m_t$ is an integer with $C_{k_{\min}}\le m_t\le C_{k_{\max}}$; (iv) the weights satisfy $S_i^t\ge 0$ and $\sum_{i\in C_k^t}S_i^t=1$.

\textit{Proof.} (i) $F_i^t\ge 1$ gives $\lambda F_i^t\ge\lambda$, and the clip in Eq.~(8) bounds $a_i^t$. (ii) $r_i^t\le\sum_j r_j^t=N\,\overline{r^t}$, hence $F_i^t=1+r_i^t/(1+\overline{r^t})<1+N$. (iii) and (iv) follow from the clamping and rounding of Eq.~(16) and from the two branches of Eq.~(18). \hfill$\square$

\textbf{Proposition 2 (bounded waiting).} Assume $m_t\ge C_{k_{\min}}$ in every committed round. With the guard, every client is selected within $W=R+\lceil N/C_{k_{\min}}\rceil$ consecutive committed rounds, i.e. $r_i^t\le W-1$ for all $i$ and $t$.

\textit{Proof.} Let client $i$ first reach $r_i^{t_0}=R$; from $t_0$ on it is overdue until it is selected. Let $A^t$ be the number of overdue clients ranked ahead of $i$, so $A^{t_0}\le N-1$. A client that becomes overdue after $t_0$ has a smaller counter than $i$ and ranks behind it, and clients ahead of $i$ that are not selected keep their order because all counters grow by one. In a round in which $i$ is not selected, all $m_t\ge C_{k_{\min}}$ selected clients are ahead of $i$, so $A^t$ falls by at least $C_{k_{\min}}$; once $A^t+1\le m_t$ the client is selected. Hence $i$ is selected at a round $t_0+k$ with $k\le\lceil N/C_{k_{\min}}\rceil-1$, when its counter is $R+k\le W-1$. \hfill$\square$

For $N=100$ and $C_{k_{\min}}=5$ the threshold is $R=20$ and no client waits more than 39 rounds, whatever the scores are. The longest waiting times observed were 6, 17, 22 and 43 rounds for $N=50,100,200,400$ (thresholds $R=10,20,40,80$), so the guard was never active in the 84 FedFACS runs (nor in the 45 runs of its A2 variant) of Section 5, and the reported results are those of the unguarded rule. The guarantee concerns participation, not influence: a selected client with $S_i^t=0$ does not change the aggregate.

\textbf{Proposition 3 (bounded round-to-round movement).} Let local training clip the gradient norm at $G$, use learning rate $\eta$ and at most $K$ local steps per round. Then $\|w_i^t-w_{\text{global}}^t\|\le\eta KG$ for every client, and, for any selection and any weights with $S_i^t\ge 0$ and $\sum_i S_i^t=1$, $\|w_{\text{global}}^{t+1}-w_{\text{global}}^t\|\le\eta KG$.

\textit{Proof.} Each clipped step moves the parameters by at most $\eta G$, so $K$ steps move them by at most $\eta KG$; the aggregate is a convex combination of the local models, and the norm is convex. \hfill$\square$

The aggregate therefore cannot move by more than $\eta KG$ in one round, whichever clients are selected or how they are weighted; clients whose update is not finite are excluded, and a round is committed only if all checks pass (Section 4.1).

\textbf{Scope.} We do not derive a convergence rate for FedFACS, which combines a heuristic selection rule with non-convex local training; convergence is evaluated empirically in Section 5, and a rate for the full method is left for future work.

\section{Experimental Evaluation}\label{sec5}

\subsection{Datasets}

For performance evaluation of the proposed framework, extensive experimental evaluations were carried out using four widely used benchmark multimedia datasets. These datasets include MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and the COVID-19 Radiography dataset. MNIST (LeCun et al. 2010) and FMNIST (Xiao et al. 2017) contain 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images, with each sample represented as a 28 \ensuremath{\times} 28 grayscale image. MNIST covers handwritten digit recognition, while FMNIST consists of images from ten clothing-related categories. In addition, CIFAR-10 extends the evaluation to natural RGB images, comprising 60,000 samples of size 32 \ensuremath{\times} 32 pixels organized into ten categories (Krizhevsky and Hinton 2009). To extend the evaluation, the COVID-19 radiography database was used to assess the framework under a real-world medical imaging scenario. It comprises chest radiographs from three classes: COVID-19, normal, and viral pneumonia (Rahman et al. 2020).  

To assess the proposed framework under heterogeneous data conditions, the training data are partitioned using four distinct scenarios to model varying degrees data heterogeneity across clients. In the first scenario (S1), a Dirichlet distribution $\mathrm{\textit{Dir}}(\alpha)$ is applied to distribute training samples among clients with the distribution parameter $\alpha \in \{0.1, 0.5\}$ to generate imbalanced datasets in both size and label distribution, where a smaller value of $\alpha$ leads to higher data skewness (Iyer. 2023). In the second scenario (S2), clients are randomly assigned data from two classes (Zhai et al. 2024). In the third scenario (S3), a number of noisy data is generated and distributed across the clients with a noise level ranging from 0\% to 45\% per client under IID conditions. In the fourth scenario (S4), three clients contain data from all ten classes with noise levels of 10\% and 20\%, while the remaining clients contain data from only nine classes with the noise patterns described in S3, under non-IID conditions (Shi et al. 2023).

\subsection{Model and experimental setup}

\textbf{Benchmark.} The comparisons are made across established federated learning baselines and recent adaptive selection methods. The proposed FedFACS framework is compared against several approaches, such as FedAvg (McMahan et al. 2017), FedProx (Li et al. 2020), DivFL (Balakrishnan et al. 2022), Power-of-Choice (Cho et al. 2022), and the approach introduced by Zhai et al. (2024) to evaluate performance and communication efficiency. 

Furthermore, FedFACS is compared against a Random baseline that selects clients randomly in each communication round, Power-of-Choice, and AHIBCS (Liu et al. 2025), a recent adaptive selection method. This comparison specifically evaluates the accuracy and convergence speed of FedFACS against the most closely related existing selection strategy, thereby validating the robustness of the presented framework.

In addition, for evaluating the balance between fairness and performance, the proposed approach is compared against four client selection strategies: a Random baseline, a Greedy strategy that prioritizes clients with the highest reputation, the RBFF method proposed by Song et al. (2022), and the FairFedCS approach introduced by Shi et al. (2023).

\textbf{Model}. The proposed FedFACS approach was implemented in Python using PyTorch and Torch-vision, employing a fine-tuned ResNet-18 (He et al. 2016) to achieve stable training. This architecture delivers high accuracy with low computational complexity, where the early blocks including the convolutional layer 1 and layers 1-3 are frozen, while the layer 4 and the final fully connected layer are trained and adjusted for 10 classes.

\textbf{Hyperparameters}. The experimental evaluation is conducted under three distinct configurations, each is designed to test the proposed model under different conditions. For configuration A, all the methods follow the same hyperparameter settings as in (Zhai et al. 2024). The federated learning environment is simulated with a single centralized server and 100 decentralized clients. The experiments are carried out for 200 training rounds, under a local training setup consisting of 10 epochs, a batch size of 32, $\beta = 0.9$, and the maximum client sampling rate $C_{k\max}$= 0.1. The models were trained via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), with learning rates of 0.05 and 0.01 are adopted for CIFAR-10 and both FMNIST and MNIST, respectively. The proximal coefficient in FedProx is set to 0.1. For the Power-of-Choice (Pow-D), 10 highest-loss clients are selected out of a randomly sampled set of 20. These experiments are to compare the proposed model against FedAvg, FedProx, Power-of-Choice, and the approach of (Zhai et al. 2024), highlighting the performance and communication efficiency under data distributions described in scenarios 1 and 2.

"""Relative-efficiency cohort rule (a2_relcoh) against the absolute rule (abl_A2): dataset x seed paired comparison."""
import glob
import json
import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\fedfacs_repro")
import numpy as np

from analyze import jain, paired

R = r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\fedfacs_repro\results"
D = {}
for f in glob.glob(os.path.join(R, "*.json")):
    r = json.load(open(f))
    c = r["cfg"]
    D[(c["method"], c["dataset"], c["scenario"], c["seed"])] = r


def met(r):
    lg = r["log"]
    va, ta = np.array(lg["val_acc"]), np.array(lg["test_acc"])
    sc = np.array(r["sel_count"], float)
    co = np.array(lg["cohort"], float)
    return dict(best=ta[int(va.argmax())] * 100, last10=ta[-10:].mean() * 100, jfi=jain(sc), never=(sc == 0).mean() * 100,
                wait=max(r["max_wait"]), cohort=co.mean(), cmin=co.min(), cmax=co.max(), at_cmax=(co == 10).mean() * 100,
                up=lg["up"][-1] / 1e9, steps=lg["steps"][-1] / 1e6, jitter=np.abs(np.diff(ta[-30:])).mean() * 100,
                val_loss=np.array(lg["val_loss"])[-1])


out = {}
cells = [(d, "s1_0.5", s) for d in ("cifar10", "fmnist") for s in (0, 1, 2)]
rows = {"abl_A2": [], "a2_relcoh": []}
for cell in cells:
    for m in rows:
        r = D.get((m,) + cell)
        if r is None:
            print("missing", m, cell)
        else:
            rows[m].append(met(r))
n = min(len(rows["abl_A2"]), len(rows["a2_relcoh"]))
print("pairs", n)
for k in ("best", "last10", "jfi", "never", "wait", "cohort", "cmin", "at_cmax", "up", "jitter"):
    a = [x[k] for x in rows["a2_relcoh"][:n]]
    b = [x[k] for x in rows["abl_A2"][:n]]
    dm, ci = paired(a, b)
    print("%-8s relcoh %.3f | abs-rule %.3f | diff %+.3f [%+.3f, %+.3f]" % (k, np.mean(a), np.mean(b), dm, ci[0], ci[1]))
    out[k] = dict(rel=float(np.mean(a)), abs=float(np.mean(b)), diff=dm, lo=ci[0], hi=ci[1])
rel = rows["a2_relcoh"]
print("relcoh cohort range over runs: min of mins", min(x["cmin"] for x in rel), "max of maxes", max(x["cmax"] for x in rel))
print("saving vs fixed cohort of 10: relcoh %.1f%%  abs %.1f%%" % (100 * (1 - np.mean([x["cohort"] for x in rel]) / 10), 100 * (1 - np.mean([x["cohort"] for x in rows["abl_A2"]]) / 10)))
# per-dataset
for ds in ("cifar10", "fmnist"):
    sub = [met(D[("a2_relcoh", ds, "s1_0.5", s)]) for s in (0, 1, 2) if ("a2_relcoh", ds, "s1_0.5", s) in D]
    sa = [met(D[("abl_A2", ds, "s1_0.5", s)]) for s in (0, 1, 2) if ("a2_relcoh", ds, "s1_0.5", s) in D]
    if sub:
        print(ds, "relcoh cohort %.2f best %.2f last10 %.2f | A2 cohort %.2f best %.2f last10 %.2f" % (np.mean([x["cohort"] for x in sub]), np.mean([x["best"] for x in sub]), np.mean([x["last10"] for x in sub]), np.mean([x["cohort"] for x in sa]), np.mean([x["best"] for x in sa]), np.mean([x["last10"] for x in sa])))
json.dump(out, open(r"C:\Users\0xRay\Downloads\paper\tools\_work\relcoh.json", "w"))

On a turn that another session's message or an automated event started, the app refuses a start: propose instead; the one exception is a `<side-sessions-event>` turn right after the user's own turn here (or another such turn), where a step they asked to have in its own session may start, in this project only.
- A follow-up you name gets a button, not just a sentence: when your reply tells the user that some work is a follow-up, a separate PR or for later, and it is real work worth doing next (not a one-line tweak or speculation), put it to them before you end the turn. This holds for a turn that only answered a question. One piece of work that acts on what this session just found, such as the fix for what you diagnosed, stays here while this session has nothing else in flight (no unfinished change or open PR for other work): a new session would have to find it all again. Ask with `wrap_up` (its question, and a button that has you do it here; in your last line where you have no `wrap_up`), write no brief, and do it on their yes. Any other that is a task of its own gets a card, whether or not you call `wrap_up`: `start_session` "own_initiative" with a complete brief. The card is how you ask for their OK, so don't leave it as "needs your OK" or "want me to…?" in prose. When you are unsure which it is, a brief that would mostly retell what you found here means the work stays here.
- After the user accepts your plan (`ExitPlanMode`), check whether two or more of its steps are real work (not "Quick things") that can each run on its own — none needs another step's result, none needs changes this session has already made, none is needed by another step, none touches files another step touches, and none must land in one change with another. A last step that only checks the finished work, such as running the tests, doesn't count: leave it out when deciding this. When at least two steps pass, the user has not said where to run them, and this turn is not one that another session's message or an automated event started, then before you begin any step: say in one line which step you are starting on and which can run at the same time, each in its own session, and propose each of those except the one you are starting on — `start_session` "own_initiative", "fresh", one card per step, at most four (any further ones you do here), each brief covering only that step. Where this session has no worktree, a new session may share this session's folder, so each brief adds: if you are working in <this folder's path> itself, touch only this step's files, commit nothing, switch no branch. These cards are the one exception to what a session and "own_initiative" are for (in this prompt and in the tool's description) and to how many cards a turn may show; they need no title line or chapter mark. Then begin your step at once: do not wait for an answer. Right before you begin a step you proposed, call `mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task` with its task_id: skip the step only if the result says it was started or is being started and the user has not told you to do it here; otherwise, do it here. A skipped step stays pending on your task list. If you skipped a step, then once your own steps are done, check `mcp__ccd_session_mgmt__list_sessions` {"linked": true}. If a skipped step's session is running or starting, say so in one line with what is left, and end your turn (the app continues you once no session started from this one is working). Otherwise, look at what each skipped step's session left (its files, branch or PR): a step whose session has nothing to show is yours again, so say so in one line and do it here. A skipped step with no session in the list may be running in a cloud session, which never reports back: say so in one line and leave it. Never do a step here if its session is waiting for the user's answer. Run the checking step last, saying what it could not cover (a session in its own worktree keeps its changes on its own branch).
- A NEW user message about something else while you are mid-task → hand the task off, then answer them (in a worktree, commit first: the new session starts from your branch tip). A small correction → just adjust. "Keep going here" → keep it here.
- Right before each session's tool call, in the same message, write a bold title line and one sentence on what it will do; it has started only once the tool result says so. Two or more at once: call `mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter` first with a short batch title.
- `context` is your call, never the user's: "fork" (gets this whole conversation) for a task that leans on this conversation while it is short; "fresh" for a self-contained one, or once it is long. Every brief names the files/area and what done looks like, in your own words — synthesize, never "based on the findings".
- A session that only reads can share this checkout (`use_worktree: false`, where this session allows it), usually on a cheaper `model`; keep yours for design-heavy work. In a worktree session `use_worktree: false` starts the new session inside this session's worktree (its branch and PR, archived with it), so never pass it for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository. At another place the user named (`cwd`, `host` or `preset`) `use_worktree: false` is that folder as it is, and this rule does not apply. Sessions that write code go one at a time per set of files — two writers never touch the same files. A `use_worktree: false` session can edit here too and nothing stops an overwrite, so when its edits may overlap yours or another session's, give it `use_worktree: true`.
- `target: "cloud"` only when the user asks for NEW work in the cloud ("run that in the cloud"): the app creates it and tells the user if it can't (no GitHub repo / no cloud environment). It starts from this session's pushed branch when in a worktree (commit and push first), else from the repository's default branch — say which in the brief.
- Somewhere else, only when the user names the place ("on my devbox", "in the api repo", "in the staging environment", "with my usual preset"), "fresh" only: `cwd` for another folder, `target: "ssh"` + `host` for one of their SSH connections, `environment` or `repository` (another GitHub repository, "owner/name") with target "cloud", or `preset`; `source_branch` / `branch_name` pick the new worktree's base and name. Take the names from `mcp__ccd_session__list_start_targets` (a repository's from the user's words or a listing that shows it), never a guess or an address; the app checks the folder and may ask the user first (a card, or to trust the folder), and a refusal in the tool result is final for this turn unless it says what to pass instead.
